content:
Your Camera Is Online. Is the Video Still Live?

A connected session tells you much less than an advancing video stream.

The connection is healthy. The frames still have somewhere to go.

A camera can answer requests while its video stops moving. A relay can receive packets while a viewer gets no new frames. A player can run smoothly while showing video that is several seconds old.

All three can sit behind the same green “online” label.

I’ve worked on video systems that bridge camera protocols, native services, and browser playback. One thing I want from their monitoring is a clear answer to a small question: where did progress stop?

That answer needs more than a successful connection or a running process. It needs evidence from the media path.

Here is how I would build that evidence, using transport, timing, decoding, and playback signals. The goal is to detect delivery problems without interpreting what appears in the picture.

Give “online” a smaller meaning

An online state can be useful. It might mean the service recently contacted the camera, an RTSP session exists, or the transport remains connected.

Keep that meaning. Add separate observations for the video.

The path might contain a camera, an ingest service, a relay, a recorder, and a browser. Each can be running while the next stage waits. A status endpoint only proves whatever work the endpoint actually checks.

MediaMTX provides a useful example of separate transport observations. Its metrics include session state, inbound and outbound traffic, RTP packet loss, and packet errors. These give more detail than a connection count alone. 1

They still describe the server’s view. A relay that forwards compressed video without decoding it cannot report whether a downstream decoder produced a usable frame. A server that sent bytes cannot prove the browser presented them.

Keep those limits visible. “Receiving video packets” is an honest and useful status. Calling it “live playback healthy” adds a claim that needs another measurement.

Track the last useful progress at each stage

For each active stream, record when useful work last advanced. The exact measurements depend on what the application does, but the questions are stable:

StageEvidence of progressWhat it does not proveIngestNew video media packets arriveA complete frame can be decodedDecodeThe decoder produces another frameThe viewer presents itPlaybackA new frame is submitted for presentationIt was captured recentlyRecordingRecorded media time advances in completed outputThat output survives every storage failureMonitoringA fresh observation arrivesThe stream itself is healthy

Keep audio and video separate. Audio packets can continue while the video track stalls. Keep control traffic separate too; a keepalive is not video progress.

For a local stage, the basic age calculation is small:

progress age = current monotonic time - last local progress time
Auto (SQL)

Both times must come from the same clock domain. A monotonic clock measures elapsed time without depending on wall-clock corrections. Raw monotonic timestamps from different machines cannot be subtracted this way.

A stage that has never produced output needs a startup state, not a fabricated “last frame” timestamp. After a reconnect, begin a new observation period and retain the previous failure in the history.

This turns a vague complaint into something you can inspect. In a constructed example, packets and decoded frames keep advancing, while presentation has not advanced for several seconds. I would first investigate the path from decoded output to the player. Restarting the camera would be a poorly targeted first response.

Smooth playback can still be late

There are two different questions: is video advancing, and how old is it?

A player can display 30 frames per second from a queue that is three seconds behind the source. Its frame rate looks healthy. Its live delay does not.

You need an age measurement to tell those cases apart. Unfortunately, a media timestamp is not automatically a capture time you can subtract from the current clock.

RTP timestamps use a media clock with an arbitrary starting point. RTCP sender reports can associate an RTP timestamp with an NTP-format timestamp, but that mapping still depends on the sender’s clock and timestamp behavior. Jitter measures variation in transit timing; it is not a measurement of total end-to-end delay. 2

Name each measured delay after its actual endpoints. “Time from gateway ingest to gateway output” is useful. Calling it “camera-to-screen latency” would hide the time spent before and after the gateway.

Where a trustworthy capture-time mapping is available, use it and document its limits. Where it is missing, track local queue age and stage delay, and leave absolute capture freshness unknown.

An honest partial measurement gives an operator somewhere to start. A precise-looking number built from unrelated clocks can send the investigation in the wrong direction.

There is another limit worth stating. A camera could repeatedly encode the same picture while sending valid packets and advancing timestamps. Transport and timing signals alone cannot reliably distinguish that from a legitimate still scene. This monitoring design detects delivery and progress failures; it does not establish whether the pictured scene is changing.

Measure the player’s side of the connection

For WebRTC playback, the statistics API exposes several stages separately. Received frames, decoded frames, packet timing, and rendering-related freeze or pause measurements can help narrow down a problem. Availability needs checking in the browsers you support. 3

Some of those measurements describe completed intervals. The specification updates pause and freeze information around rendered frames; a pause count increments when rendering resumes after the pause. I would not rely on that counter alone to detect a stall that is still happening. 3

The page needs a current progress observation as well.

requestVideoFrameCallback() runs when a new frame is sent to the compositor and exposes presentation-related metadata. It can help track whether the video element is advancing. The callback runs on the main thread, and the API does not guarantee exact synchronization with physical display output. 4

That distinction matters during diagnosis. If the page’s main thread is blocked, the callback can be late too. If the user paused playback or the page is in the background, the application’s expectations need to change.

Report playback intent and page state alongside the timing. “Expected to play, visible, no presentation progress” is much more useful than “no callback.”

Client reports also have a delivery path of their own. If those reports stop reaching the backend, the backend has lost visibility. It has not proved that the camera stopped sending video.

Turn observations into states carefully

A single timeout for every stream is tempting. It also ignores how streams behave.

A low-frame-rate source has a different expected gap from a 30 fps preview. A newly connected decoder may need time to produce its first frame. An on-demand stream may correctly be idle until someone starts watching it.

Begin with explicit expectations for each stream class: whether media should be flowing, how often progress is expected, and how much startup time is allowed.

The active stream can then move between a few states:

Starting: the stream is expected, but it has not established normal progress yet.
Healthy: the required observations are fresh and within their budgets.
Degraded: progress continues, but a delay or error budget is exceeded.
Stalled: an expected stage has stopped advancing beyond its allowed gap.
Unknown: the observations needed to make the decision are missing or stale.

An intentionally idle stream sits outside the active-stream evaluation. It should not create a stream failure merely because no viewer requested it.

The thresholds should come from the service requirement and the stream’s expected behavior. I would record the reason for every transition: ingest stopped, decode stopped, presentation stopped, or delay grew too large.

Require sustained recovery before clearing an alert. One packet after a long silence is evidence of contact, but it does not establish stable playback.

The classifier itself should not have to watch every frame centrally. Each component can maintain its local progress and send compact summaries. Detailed timing can be retained around a transition, when it is most useful for diagnosis.

Read counters across a useful interval

A total packet-loss counter answers how much loss has accumulated over its lifetime. The change over a recent interval helps answer what is happening now.

Compare observations from the same stream session. A reconnect, process restart, or replacement statistics object can reset a counter. Keep the session identity with the samples and start a new baseline when it changes. Do not treat a reset as a sudden negative rate or uninterrupted success.

Preserve incident history outside the live session object. Reconnecting can restore the stream while making its new counters look perfectly clean.

Loss, jitter, and errors help explain degraded delivery, but no single one is a universal failure threshold. A receiver may recover some lost data. A stream can also stall without packet loss if a downstream stage stops consuming it.

GStreamer’s RTP jitter buffer illustrates the tradeoff: it reorders packets and waits within a configured latency budget. Waiting can help with late arrivals, while adding delay to the path. Its settings and drop observations belong in the investigation. 5

Look for changes together: rising queue age, slower decode output, late packets, and stalled presentation. Agreement between independent observations is more useful than a red threshold on an isolated graph.

Recording needs its own health signal

A live viewer and a recorder can fail independently. A healthy player does not prove the recording is progressing, and a growing file does not prove the latest video is available for playback.

For a segmented recorder, I would track the most recently completed segment, the media interval it covers, and whether it can be opened and decoded. I would separately track whether that segment reached the intended storage destination.

This check does not need to interpret the frames. It checks the container, timestamps, and decodability. It should also account for audio-only progress rather than assuming any file growth means new video was saved.

The expected completion interval depends on the recording format and segment policy. An unfinished segment can be normal. A health rule that ignores that will produce false alarms at regular intervals.

A slow recorder can also affect another branch if they share work or buffers. GStreamer’s tee documentation calls for a separate queue or multiqueue in each branch so a blocked branch does not immediately stall the others. Finite queues still need an overload policy once they fill. 6

Missing recorded time should be explicit. Buffering, rejected work, and storage failure should lead to a visible result that the operator can distinguish from a complete recording.

Test the green status, not just the reconnect

Before trusting these states, I would create failures in a small test setup and check the reported timeline.

Start with a sender that can stop video while keeping its control path alive. The expected result is a media-progress failure even if the connection stays open.

Then hold packets long enough to create delay while allowing them to keep arriving. Check that advancing counters do not hide old video. Slow a downstream consumer separately, so the monitoring can distinguish ingest progress from output progress.

Test a slow recording destination while watching live playback. Pause the player deliberately. Put the page in the background. Stop the component that reports metrics. Each case should produce a reason that matches what actually happened, including “unknown” when observation is lost.

Finally, reconnect the stream and let it recover. Check startup handling, reset counters, alert clearing, and retention of the previous gap. A test that ends at the first successful reconnect misses much of the behavior an operator will depend on.

These tests establish what the health labels mean. They also expose cases where the application does not yet have enough information to make a reliable claim.

I would still keep the small green connection light. Beside it, I would want to see where video last advanced, how much delay we can actually measure, and when those observations were updated.

That gives the next engineer something better than “the camera is online.” It gives them a place to look.

Sources
MediaMTX: Extract metrics.
RFC 3550: RTP — A Transport Protocol for Real-Time Applications, especially sections 5.1 and 6.4.1.
W3C: Identifiers for WebRTC’s Statistics API, including inbound RTP and video pause/freeze definitions.
MDN: HTMLVideoElement.requestVideoFrameCallback().
GStreamer: rtpjitterbuffer.
GStreamer: tee.

I’m Burak Hamuryen, a software engineer in Berlin working on distributed systems and real-time video infrastructure. More at hamuryen.com.

content:
4 Years, 6 Languages, 1 Monorepo: What I’d Do Differently

Shared code made integration easier. Keeping everyday work fast took more care.

One place to change the system. Different parts to build, test, and release.

Over roughly four years, I worked in a monorepo with six languages and around 20 to 30 services and components. There were backend services, plugins, web applications, and AI components. They shared a repository, but they did not all behave like the same kind of project.

The clearest benefit was integration.

When a model or DTO changed, it was easier to find the affected code and update it together. A DTO is the object used to carry data between parts of a system. Changing its shape can mean changing a producer, a consumer, tests, and sometimes a user interface.

Having those pieces in one place reduced the risk of overlooking an incompatible change. I could look at the whole change instead of reconstructing it across several repositories and pull requests.

I also remember waiting. Tests and hooks took time. Changes around base layers brought in tests far from the task I was working on. Commits arrived from unrelated parts of the repository. Keeping standards consistent needed attention, and changes to the release structure needed following.

Both sides belong in the story. I would want to keep the integration benefit. I would put more deliberate work into the daily cost of sharing the repository.

Keep the cross-service change visible

Consider a small example: a backend adds a field to a response, a plugin reads it, and a web application displays it.

In one repository, the pull request can show the producer, the consumers, and the tests together. A reviewer can follow the field from its definition to its use. If code generation is involved, the schema and generated clients can be checked as part of the same change.

That does not prove the feature works. It does make some missing pieces easier to notice. The plugin may still expect the old field name. A test fixture may use the wrong type. The web application may assume a value is always present.

This is the part of a monorepo I would protect. Moving everything apart just to make each directory quieter can introduce another cost: coordinating changes that used to be visible in one diff.

That visibility should help reviewers too. A contract change should explain which components produce it, which consume it, and which versions may coexist. A large pull request containing all the code still needs a readable explanation of the dependency between its parts.

The repository gives you a convenient place to inspect integration. The review process has to use it.

“Unrelated to my task” is not always “unaffected”

One frustrating part was seeing tests run in areas that seemed unrelated to the change I wanted to make.

There are two different problems hiding there.

A test may run because the pipeline selects too much work. It may also run because a shared base layer really does connect those areas. In the second case, skipping the test would hide the dependency without removing it.

Today, my first question would be why a target was selected. Which changed input led to this test? Was it a source dependency, a generated file, a compiler setting, or a global configuration change?

Pants documents the difference between checking changed files and including their dependents. Its CI guide uses transitive changed dependents for checks that need to account for downstream effects, and it calls out cases where configuration changes need broader validation. 1

That is a useful principle even when the repository uses another build tool. Directory filters alone are a weak model of how software depends on other software.

In a repository with several build systems, the boundaries between their graphs need checking too. If a schema change feeds generated code in another language, that edge must exist somewhere the CI selection process understands. Each tool can be correct about its own targets while the overall pipeline still misses a consumer.

The goal would be a test selection I can explain and trust. On changes where the graph is incomplete or a shared toolchain changes, a broader run is reasonable.

Give the base layer a smaller job

A shared layer is attractive because another service already needs something similar. Over time, it can become a convenient home for things that have little in common.

Logging helpers arrive beside domain models. A small utility gains a dependency on a large client library. More services import the package because they need one function from it.

Then a small edit reaches further than expected.

I would review heavily shared packages by asking what their consumers actually need. Can stable protocol definitions stand on their own? Can a small utility avoid pulling in application-specific code? Does a domain rule belong with its owning service instead of the lowest common layer?

I would not split every helper into a separate package. That has its own maintenance cost. I would start with dependencies that repeatedly widen builds and tests, or make an otherwise local change difficult to release.

This is where the waiting becomes useful evidence. A slow CI job may be a tooling problem. It may also be showing you that the code has become more connected than the team intended.

Renaming a directory will not change that. Narrowing a real dependency can.

Put short feedback close to the edit

Long hooks were another recurring irritation. A commit is a small action in a developer’s day. Attaching too much work to it makes the cost appear again and again.

If I were setting the policy today, I would give local checks a clear purpose: catch cheap, obvious mistakes quickly. Formatting, basic linting, and selected fast checks fit that purpose. A broad integration suite usually needs another place to run.

The pre-commit framework supports file filters and hook stages, so hooks do not all need to run on every file at the same point in the workflow. Its configuration also supports pinned hook revisions. 2

The harder decision is what to put behind those settings. I would ask developers to run a small relevant test target while editing, keep commit-time work predictable, and let required CI checks enforce the wider policy before merging.

Local hooks are useful feedback, but they can be bypassed or missing. They should not be the only place a required check exists.

Waiting for a runner deserves its own measurement. To a developer, queue time and execution time are both time lost. Adding a cache does not help much if most of the wait happens before the build begins.

The measurement I would keep is time from a change to actionable feedback, including slower cases. A collection of impressive individual job times can still produce an unpleasant working day.

Cache results only when the inputs are understood

A shared build cache can remove repeated work across machines. In a repository this size, that is worth taking seriously.

It is also worth understanding what makes a result reusable.

Bazel’s remote cache works with build actions and their declared inputs and outputs. Its documentation warns about tools outside the workspace that are not tracked as inputs. A cache cannot account for a relevant dependency that the build description leaves out. 3

Compiler and tool versions, generator inputs, environment dependencies, and lockfiles all deserve checking before a high cache-hit rate counts as success. A fast result is only useful if it belongs to the current inputs.

Clean and warm builds need separate measurements, with attention to the jobs that determine the overall completion time. Saving work on many small targets may barely change the time a developer waits for one long, uncached integration job.

This would also make cache failures easier to discuss. “The cache did not help this change” is more useful when we know whether the cause was changed inputs, missing entries, download time, or a job that could never reuse a result in the first place.

Make Git easier to read and cheaper to use

The repository had a steady flow of commits from parts of the system unrelated to my immediate work. Following that traffic made everyday Git work harder.

Some of that was an attention problem. The amount of data in a large repository raises a different set of questions.

For attention, path-limited history helps when investigating one area. For example, with illustrative directory names:

git log --oneline -- services/payments/ packages/contracts/
Auto (Bash)

Git supports limiting history by paths. That gives me a more focused view; it does not create an independent branch history or remove dependencies outside those paths. 4

For large checkouts, sparse checkout and partial clone address different costs. Sparse checkout limits the working-tree paths present locally. A partial clone using a filter such as blob:none can defer downloading file contents until needed, when supported by the server. Neither feature removes everyone else's commits from the repository's history. 5 6

I would test these with the actual build workflow before recommending them to the whole team. A convenient small checkout stops being convenient if code generation expects missing directories or a build immediately downloads everything anyway.

More commits also do not automatically mean more conflicts. Edits to independent files often merge cleanly. The difficult cases deserve attention of their own: shared configuration, lockfiles, generated outputs, and changes that cross the same interfaces.

Share standards without forcing identical tooling

Six languages need consistent expectations. They do not need the same formatter or the same test runner.

A small common set of requirements would be my starting point: an obvious build command, a test entry point, a named owner, dependency update rules, and a documented release path. Each language can meet those requirements with tools that suit it.

Shared configuration needs ownership too. A change to a root hook, base image, or code generator can affect people who never touch its directory. Someone should understand that reach and be responsible for reviewing changes to it.

CODEOWNERS can help route reviews. On GitHub, requiring approval from code owners is a separate branch protection setting; simply adding the file does not enforce that approval. 7

I would prefer a few enforced expectations with clear owners over a long standards document that depends on everyone remembering to read it.

One commit still has to survive several releases

The biggest limit of the integration benefit appears after merging.

A backend service, a plugin, and a web application can be correct together in one commit and still reach their users at different times. A plugin may remain on an older version while the backend moves forward. A rollback can bring an older consumer back into use.

This is why I would make release compatibility part of the contract review.

Protocol Buffers gives concrete examples: adding fields can be safe for binary wire compatibility, while reusing field numbers is dangerous. It also distinguishes binary compatibility from source-level and application concerns. Successful parsing does not prove that two versions agree on meaning. 8

For an illustrative change from timeout_seconds to timeout_ms, I would introduce the new field alongside the old one and define which value takes precedence. Readers would learn the new field while still accepting the old representation. Writers would keep supporting older consumers during the transition. Removal would wait until the supported version combinations no longer need the old field.

Those tests need rollback combinations too. Testing only the newest producer with the newest consumer misses the period when releases overlap.

Release records should make that overlap visible: which artifact was deployed, which commit produced it, and which contract versions it supports. If the release process changes, that information should remain easy to find.

Sharing a Git repository is a weak reason to release every component together. When two components depend on being released in a particular order, that dependency needs to be explicit.

What I would keep

I would keep the ability to follow an integration change across the system in one place. It helped when models and DTOs changed, and it reduced the chance of leaving a consumer behind.

I would spend more effort on the costs that arrive every day: broad test selection, heavy base layers, long hooks, noisy history, and release tracking. Those are easy to postpone because each one looks manageable on its own.

Together, they shape how pleasant the repository is to work in.

The question I would bring to the next monorepo is simple: when one small thing changes, how much of the system should a developer have to think about?

I want the rest to remain available when I need it. I don’t want every edit to require understanding all of it.

content:
Before Buying More GPUs, Fix Your Video Pipeline

The expensive part may be getting frames to the GPU, keeping them there, and moving them out on time.

A faster GPU cannot remove a queue somewhere else in the pipeline.

Take a video service that starts falling behind as more streams arrive. Playback gets later. Memory usage climbs. Someone opens a capacity request for another GPU machine.

That might be the right purchase. I would still want to follow one frame through the service before approving it.

Where does it wait? Which thread moves it forward? How many times does it cross between CPU and GPU memory? What happens when the destination cannot accept it?

I’ve worked on native video systems and RTSP-to-WebRTC bridges. That background makes me interested in the gaps between the named components. A diagram can say “hardware decode” and “hardware encode” while leaving out a download, a CPU filter, an upload, and a blocking write between them.

Those gaps deserve a place in the capacity discussion.

Start with the video you actually need

Before measuring a pipeline, write down its output requirements.

A live preview needs recent frames. A recording needs a clear policy for preserving video and reporting gaps. An offline export might mainly need to finish quickly. These jobs can share code, but their definitions of success are different.

For a live service, specify the expected resolution, frame rate, codec, and acceptable delay. Decide what can happen under overload too. Can the preview skip frames? Can the source lower its bitrate? When must the service reject another stream?

Without those decisions, “supports more streams” is an incomplete result. A service that accepts every connection but delivers video several seconds late may already be over capacity.

Then ask whether the job needs decoded frames at all.

FFmpeg’s stream-copy path transfers encoded packets without decoding and encoding them again. When the destination accepts the existing codec and stream parameters, remuxing into a suitable container can avoid that work. It does not support filters that need decoded frames, and container compatibility still matters. 1

A recording or relay path is worth checking here. Decoding video just to encode the same thing again should be a deliberate choice. Perhaps the output needs another codec, resolution, or bitrate. Perhaps it doesn’t.

Draw the memory path

A useful pipeline sketch shows more than component names:

encoded packets
    -> hardware decoder
    -> decoded frames in GPU memory
    -> resize or format conversion, if needed
    -> hardware encoder
    -> encoded packets
    -> network or storage
Auto (Rust)

Now mark every place a frame leaves GPU memory. Also mark where the code waits for another operation to finish.

In NVIDIA’s FFmpeg guide, -hwaccel cuda -hwaccel_output_format cuda selects a hardware decode path with frames kept in GPU memory. Compatible GPU filters and hardware encoding can then continue that path. A CPU filter inserted between those stages may require a download and a later upload. Check the complete filter chain and the capabilities of your installed build. 2

The raw data adds up quickly. NV12 stores 8-bit YUV 4:2:0 video at 12 bits per pixel, or 1.5 bytes per pixel before padding. 3 For a tightly packed 1920 × 1080 frame, the payload calculation is:

1920 × 1080 × 1.5 = 3,110,400 bytes per frame
3,110,400 × 30 = 93.312 MB per second
Auto (SQL)

Here, MB means one million bytes. At 30 frames per second, downloading every frame and uploading it again moves about 186.6 MB per second of raw payload per stream. Forty streams would move about 7.46 GB per second across those two directions combined.

That is arithmetic, not a benchmark. It excludes row padding, alignment, other copies, and transfer overhead. It also does not mean 7.46 GB per second travels in each direction, or that every machine will hit a bus limit at that rate.

It gives you something specific to investigate: a small CPU operation between two GPU stages can require moving a surprisingly large amount of data.

When reading native code, I would look for the reason behind each copy. Does the consumer need its own buffer? Is the format incompatible? Did a convenient library API quietly force the data through host memory? Some copies will be necessary. Others may be leftovers from an earlier design.

Check which part of the GPU is busy

“GPU utilization is low” needs a second question: which utilization?

NVIDIA’s monitoring tools distinguish general GPU activity from encoder and decoder activity. The nvidia-smi documentation also distinguishes memory utilization from the amount of allocated framebuffer memory. Metric support varies by device and configuration; an unavailable reading is not evidence that an engine is idle. 4

A video workload can put pressure on dedicated codec hardware while leaving much of the general compute capacity available. A low general GPU percentage therefore does not establish spare decoding or encoding capacity.

Collect those readings alongside CPU usage, input and output rates, transfer activity, and queue age. They need to cover the same interval. Comparing yesterday’s average GPU graph with today’s worst stream tells you very little.

The useful observation is a relationship. Perhaps output slows while encoder activity stays high. Perhaps every engine looks quiet while one CPU thread is busy. Perhaps output only falls behind when the storage destination slows down.

Each observation points to a different next measurement. None is a diagnosis by itself.

It is also worth looking at individual streams. An average can hide one expensive input format, one unstable source, or a few sessions that retain buffers much longer than the others. A fleet total is helpful for capacity planning; a per-stream timeline helps explain where that capacity went.

A frame can be waiting for its own buffer

Memory usage does not have to grow forever for buffer ownership to hurt throughput. A fixed pool can run out of available surfaces because downstream work is still holding them.

NVIDIA’s NVDEC guide makes two details explicit. cuvidMapVideoFrame() waits for decoding to complete. Calling it on the thread that submits decode work can prevent that thread from submitting more work while it waits. Mapped output surfaces must also be released with cuvidUnmapVideoFrame(); only a limited number may remain mapped. 5

For code using that API, inspect the lifetime of a surface from acquisition to release. A reference held by an encoder, a queue, or an error path can matter just as much as the allocation itself.

Returning a surface too early is not a performance fix. If asynchronous work still reads it, reuse can corrupt the result. The release point has to follow the actual completion of the last consumer.

This is one reason I like ownership to be visible in the code. A frame handle should make it possible to answer who currently owns the data and what event makes it reusable. A raw pointer passed through several callbacks makes that question harder.

Adding another worker thread can help when submission is blocked. It can also add more outstanding work to the same exhausted pool. I would measure the wait and understand the lifetime before increasing concurrency.

Bigger queues can make a live service worse

Suppose a source produces 30 frames per second and a downstream stage can sustain only 25. An unbounded queue gains five frames every second. A larger queue delays the moment when the system must deal with that mismatch.

It also lets the video get older.

For a live preview, I care about how long the oldest frame has been waiting. A queue with ten frames has a different meaning at 5 fps and 60 fps. Count and byte limits protect resources; an age limit expresses something closer to the viewing requirement.

GStreamer’s queue element supports limits and can either block or discard buffers when full, depending on its configuration. These are different overload policies, with different consequences. 6

Choose the policy at the right stage. Dropping an old decoded frame before presentation may be acceptable for a live preview. Arbitrarily dropping compressed data can damage later frames that depend on it. A recording branch needs its own decision about gaps, buffering, and failure reporting.

Give the viewer and recording writer separate branches with finite budgets. Separate threads alone do not provide lasting isolation if both branches eventually block on shared buffers or shared output work.

When a budget is exhausted, make the result observable. Count intentional drops. Report recording gaps. Reject work if necessary. A service that silently accumulates delay is difficult to operate because its failure arrives long after its capacity was exceeded.

The recent SDK work is worth reading

NVIDIA’s July 31, 2026 article about Video Codec SDK 13.1 describes updated transcoding samples with separate submission work and queues between stages. It also introduces AppTransZeroCopy, which can share suitable CUDA arrays between decode and encode instead of using an intermediate copy and conversion. 7

The interesting part is the treatment of memory ownership and scheduling as part of video performance. These are concrete examples to study when inspecting a similar path in your own application.

The sample’s benefits depend on a compatible path, including hardware, driver, format, and processing requirements. “Zero copy” in one handoff does not mean that an entire application moves no data. Nor does installing a newer SDK automatically reorganize an existing pipeline.

I would use the sample to form a specific hypothesis: perhaps this intermediate surface or synchronization point is avoidable. Then I would check that hypothesis against the application’s actual output requirements.

Measure a change you can explain

Start with a repeatable workload and keep a small record of the test conditions: GPU model, driver, FFmpeg or SDK version, codecs, resolution, frame rate, encoder settings, and destination.

The input needs to match the question. Reading a local file as quickly as possible can help measure processing capacity. It does not reproduce a live source’s pacing, reconnects, or network variation. I would use both kinds of test when the service has to handle both conditions.

Record four things together:

Useful output: completed frames or playable output at the required settings.
Delay: time spent inside measured stages and queues, including the slower cases.
Resource use: CPU, relevant GPU engines, memory, transfers, and output I/O.
Failure behavior: drops, errors, reconnects, and recovery after overload.

Local timing should use a monotonic clock. Capture-to-display delay is a separate measurement and needs a trustworthy relationship between the source and destination clocks.

Change one part of the path. Remove an unnecessary host round trip, shorten a surface lifetime, or isolate a slow output. Repeat the same workload and check output correctness as well as speed.

For diagnosis, a temporary discard sink can show whether a real output destination is holding things up. The final capacity test still needs that destination. Otherwise, the result leaves out work the deployed service must do.

Let the test run long enough to expose a growing backlog. A short burst can look healthy while its queues borrow time from the rest of the system. Recovery matters too: after input load falls, does latency return to normal, or does the service keep showing old video?

Only then would I increase stream count and look for the first requirement the service can no longer meet.

Make the hardware request specific

Sometimes the result will be clear: the required codec engine is saturated, memory capacity is insufficient, or the application needs more independent processing capacity. More hardware may be exactly the right answer.

The investigation is still useful. It tells you which resource to buy and what additional capacity to expect under the tested conditions.

Other times, a GPU spends part of its day waiting for frames, a free surface, or an output writer. Another GPU might leave those waits untouched.

Before buying it, follow one frame. Find out where its time goes.

content:
AI Agents Are Distributed Systems. Treat Them Like One.

What happens when a tool succeeds, the response gets lost, and your agent tries again?

The action succeeded. The response never arrived. What should the agent do next?

Imagine a support agent handling a refund.

It reads the ticket, checks the order, and calls the refund API. The payment service records the refund. Then the connection drops before the response gets back.

The agent sees a timeout. Retrying sounds reasonable, but the first refund may already be on its way. A second request could issue another one. Asking the model to think harder won’t tell you whether the payment service committed the transaction.

This is the part of building agents that interests me. I’ve spent much of my career working on backend services, video pipelines, and infrastructure. When I look at an agent calling several tools to finish a task, I recognize a lot of the same problems.

Once an agent calls remote tools and changes data in other services, its work spans several systems. Something can succeed in one place and fail in another. A process can die halfway through the job.

Adding a model gives that system a new way to choose its next step. The old failure modes are still there.

The timeout tells you less than you think

After a timeout, several things could have happened. The request never reached the service. The service rejected it. The refund succeeded, but the response was lost. The service might even still be processing it.

From the caller’s side, these can look exactly the same.

The refund operation needs an idempotency key: a stable ID for this particular action. Every retry sends the same key. The receiving service uses it to recognize repeat requests and avoid issuing another refund.

The important word is stable. If your tool wrapper creates a new UUID every time it runs, every retry looks like a new refund.

Application code should create and save that key before making the first request. It belongs to the business operation, with its customer, order, amount, and currency. Reusing it with different details should fail.

For example, the job might save an operation ID of refund-op-7842. All three attempts use refund-op-7842. Even if the model proposes the refund again in different words, the application must recognize the existing operation. A fresh tool call doesn't automatically mean a new business action.

AWS explains this contract in Making retries safe with idempotent APIs. Check the provider’s retention rules too. Stripe, for example, allows keys to be removed after at least 24 hours. An old job can’t assume that its key still protects it.

There is a catch: saving a key in your own database isn’t enough when the action happens somewhere else. Your worker can still crash after the external service succeeds and before you save its response.

The service performing the action needs to support deduplication, or give you a reliable way to look up what happened. An empty search result isn’t proof of failure if the first request might still be running. Some jobs need to stop for investigation. An unknown outcome is a valid state. Pretending it means “failed” can get expensive.

A chat history is a poor job database

Suppose the agent’s conversation contains this line:

I have processed the refund and will now notify the customer.

That tells you what the model said. Before showing the customer a success message, I want a receipt from the payment service.

For a job like this, I would store the proposed action, its validated inputs, the approval if one was needed, the operation ID, and the confirmed external result. The conversation can help explain the decision. The job record tells the application what it can safely do next.

This also changes how you handle a restart. A replacement worker should be able to load the job and see that the refund is confirmed but the notification is still pending. It shouldn’t have to reread a conversation and guess.

I’d keep the state names plain: proposed, approved, running, confirmed, outcome unknown, failed. Moving a refund to “confirmed” requires evidence from the payment service. A confident sentence from the model doesn’t qualify.

Put a boundary around the model’s decision

The model is useful when a request needs interpretation. A customer writes three paragraphs about a damaged item, and the agent works out which order they mean and what help they want.

Once it proposes a refund, regular application code can take over much of the work.

Does this order belong to the customer? Is the amount valid? Has it already been refunded? Does the current user have permission? Is approval required?

These checks belong at the tool boundary, where they run regardless of what the prompt says.

The flow I would start with looks like this:

Read the request
    -> Ask the model for a proposed action
    -> Validate the action in code
    -> Save the proposal and operation ID
    -> Get approval when required
    -> Execute through a controlled tool
    -> Record the confirmed result
    -> Tell the customer what happened
Auto (Rust)

This leaves the model room to handle messy language without giving it ownership of every business rule.

It also makes failure easier to explain. “The amount exceeds the allowed refund” is something you can test and show to a user. A long conversation where the model talks itself into a different amount is much harder to reason about.

Where Temporal fits

Long-running video jobs have a similar shape. A request may pass through export, processing, storage, and notification. Some steps take time. Some fail. Restarting the entire chain can repeat expensive work.

That is the kind of problem where a workflow system becomes useful.

With Temporal, I would keep the coordination in a Workflow and put model calls and external API calls in Activities. Temporal records execution history so workers can rebuild workflow state after a failure. The workflow code must be deterministic: replaying the same recorded history must produce the same sequence of commands.

The distinction matters for agents. A fresh model call can produce a different answer. During recovery, a recorded Activity result lets the workflow reuse the earlier decision. An Activity whose completion wasn’t recorded may still run again, so the uncertainty hasn’t disappeared.

Temporal also doesn’t make a refund API safe to retry. If the payment succeeds and the Activity worker dies before reporting completion, another attempt can call that API again. The Activity execution documentation covers this retry behavior. The operation ID still needs to travel all the way to the service that performs the refund.

I wouldn’t add Temporal to every agent project. For a short task with a few steps, a database job table and a worker may be enough. You still have to design job claiming, retries, and recovery, but that can be a reasonable amount of code.

Once jobs wait for people, span several services, or need careful recovery across many steps, I’d look much more closely at a workflow engine.

Human approval becomes stale

“Ask a human first” sounds like a complete solution until the human takes two days to answer.

During those two days, someone else might refund the order. The customer’s request might change. The person who started the job might lose access.

A saved approval should refer to a specific action: this order, this amount, this currency, this version of the proposal. If the proposal changes, the old approval should no longer apply.

Before execution, the system should check current permissions and business conditions again. Those checks also need protection against concurrent changes at the service performing the action. A check in the agent process alone leaves a gap between checking and doing.

I would give approvals an expiry time too. Otherwise, an old job can wake up weeks later and perform something nobody is expecting anymore.

The interface should show what is waiting, who needs to respond, and what will happen after approval. “Agent is thinking” is a bad description of a job that has been waiting for a manager since Tuesday.

Give retries an owner and a budget

An agent can retry at several levels without anyone intending it.

The HTTP client retries. The tool wrapper retries. The workflow retries the Activity. Then the model sees an error and decides to try the tool again.

If three layers each make three attempts, one logical action can turn into 27 downstream calls. During an outage, that extra load makes recovery harder.

I’d choose where retry policy lives and keep the other layers visible. Temporary failures can use bounded retries with increasing delays and jitter. Invalid input and permission failures should usually go back for correction. An uncertain write needs reconciliation before another attempt unless the receiving API can safely deduplicate it.

The agent also needs limits on the whole job: tool calls, elapsed time, model spend, and repeated attempts at the same action. AWS covers the service-side reasoning in its guidance on controlling retry calls.

The exact limits depend on the task. The application should enforce them outside the model. A prompt saying “don’t spend too much” is hard to put on a dashboard.

Debug the job from its receipts

When a customer asks why they received two notifications, the final assistant message won’t be enough.

I want to follow one job ID through the proposal, tool attempts, external requests, and results. Each attempt should have its own ID, while retries of the same business action keep the same operation ID.

Record the model and prompt version as well. They help explain why an action was proposed. Keep sensitive content out of general logs; store only what you need with appropriate access and retention.

Then measure the outcome of the job. Did the requested task finish? How long did it take? How many jobs are stuck waiting? How many have an unknown external outcome? How much did each completed task cost?

A successful model response is only one event in that chain. The payment receipt and the delivery status tell you whether the customer actually got what they asked for.

Adding more agents makes those IDs even more useful. If two agents pick up the same ticket, they need a shared way to recognize work already in progress. I’d start with one agent and add another when a specific part of the job benefits from it.

The test I’d run before shipping

Take the refund flow and make the payment service return success. Kill the worker immediately afterward, before it saves the result.

Restart it.

Does it issue another refund? Does it find the first one? Does it stop with an unknown outcome? Can you tell which happened without reading every log line?

That one test exercises a boundary that a happy-path demo never touches.

I would also run the same job on two workers, deliver the same approval twice, and change the order while approval is pending. Then make a tool time out repeatedly and check that the job eventually stops within its budget.

You can run most of these with a fake model returning a fixed proposal. That makes the recovery behavior easier to test. Separately, test the model’s decisions against examples of ambiguous requests, missing information, and actions it shouldn’t propose.

Both kinds of tests matter. A system can reliably execute the wrong decision. It can also make the right decision and lose track of the result.

Before shipping, I want an answer to this question: if the process dies after an external action, what will the next worker do?

For our refund, it loads the saved operation ID, checks the payment service, finds the existing receipt, and continues with the notification. If it can’t establish what happened, it leaves the refund alone and flags the job for review.

Once that works, I’d feel much better about letting the agent handle the next ticket.

content:
From Monolith to 15 Microservices: When It Actually Made Sense

Everyone’s writing about going back to monoliths. Here’s why we went the other way in 2013, before “microservices” was even a word we knew.

Three engineers, fifteen services, zero containers. Sometimes less infrastructure is the answer.

In May 2011, a group of software architects met at a workshop near Venice and started describing something they called “micro services.” By May 2012, they settled on the name “microservices.” Martin Fowler and James Lewis published the article that made the term mainstream in March 2014.

I didn’t read any of that. In late 2013, I was an engineer at a small defense and video analytics company going through a transition. Most of the senior engineers had left. I was mid-level with about a year of experience, but I was the most experienced developer on the team. I split a C++ application into 15 separate services because the monolithic version we’d built the year before was getting in the way.

Same idea. Different continent. No buzzwords.

The Monolith We’d Already Built

The year before, we’d built a video management system for a client. C++, Qt for the desktop frontend, PostgreSQL for the database, gSOAP for the service layer. Standard stack for the era. It was a monolith: one codebase, one build, one deployment.

It worked fine for a single client. But when we decided to build our own product, a VMS we’d sell to multiple customers and deploy on-premise at their sites, the monolith’s limits became obvious. Every change to the camera integration module required rebuilding and redeploying the entire system. Authentication code that hadn’t changed in months got retested because it shared a binary with alerting code that changed weekly. Different features had completely different update cycles, but they were all locked together.

So for the new product, I designed it differently. Not because I’d read about microservices. Because I’d experienced the monolith, and I didn’t want to do it again.

Splitting It Up

I broke the system into about 10–15 separate services. Each one was its own C++ project, its own binary, its own process:

User service: authentication, login, permissions, roles
Camera/asset service: device management, stream configuration, brand-specific integrations
Recording service: storage management, retention policies, playback
Live view service: real-time stream distribution to clients
Alerting service: rule engine, event triggers, notifications
Analytics service: video analytics processing, detection events
And several more for logging, configuration, licensing

Each service had its own PostgreSQL schema within a shared database instance. The user service owned the users schema, camera management owned assets, alerting owned alerts. They didn't reach into each other's tables. We couldn't afford to run 15 separate database instances for a product that would be deployed on whatever hardware the customer had on-premise, but the schema separation meant services stayed out of each other's data.

I built the architecture and the foundation. Then two developers joined: one junior, one with about a year of experience. Three people, 15 services.

Why We Used SOAP Instead of REST in 2013

If you’ve only ever worked with REST and JSON, brace yourself.

In 2013, SOAP was still the enterprise standard. REST was gaining ground, especially in the web world, but in C++ desktop applications talking to backend services, SOAP with gSOAP was the established tool. REST frameworks for C++ were immature or nonexistent. gSOAP gave us code generation from WSDL definitions, type-safe communication, and a protocol that worked.

It also gave us headaches.

gSOAP generates C++ code from your service definitions. You define the interface, run the generator, and get a pile of .cpp and .h files with XML serialization for every data type. For a single service calling a single other service, it works fine. Clean, structured, predictable.

The problem starts when one service needs to call multiple other services. The alerting service needed to talk to both the user service (to check permissions) and the camera service (to get device info). That meant including generated code from both services in the same project. And that’s where gSOAP broke down.

Namespace collisions. The generated code from the user service defined types and serialization functions that clashed with the generated code from the camera service. The solution was wrapping each client in its own C++ namespace, carefully isolating the generated files, and making sure nothing leaked across boundaries. It was tedious, fragile, and error-prone. Add a field to one service’s API and you’d spend an afternoon fixing compile errors in a consuming service that didn’t change at all. This was a well-documented pain point in the gSOAP community.

And then there was the XML overhead. Every call serialized data to XML, sent it over the wire, and deserialized on the other side. For the kind of data we were passing (device lists, user permissions, alert configurations), the XML payload was often 5–10x larger than the actual data. Not a disaster on a local network, but wasteful.

If I were doing it today, I’d use REST with JSON, or gRPC for the performance-sensitive paths. In 2013, those weren’t real options for C++. gSOAP was what we had, and it worked. Just not gracefully.

No Docker, No Kubernetes, No Problem

Each service ran as a Linux service on CentOS. Start, stop, restart independently. Check logs in /var/log/. That's it.

No containers. Docker had just released version 0.9 in 2013 and nobody in our world had heard of it. Kubernetes didn’t exist yet (Google released it in 2014). We didn’t have service discovery, load balancing, or health checks. Services found each other through configuration files that listed IP addresses and ports.

Deployment meant updating one binary on the customer’s server and restarting that one systemd service. When we needed to update the alerting service, we updated the alerting service. The camera service kept running. The user service kept running. No coordinated restart, no deployment pipeline, no downtime.

For on-premise deployments to customers who didn’t have cloud infrastructure (cloud wasn’t really an option for most of our customers in 2013), this simplicity was the whole point. The product ran on whatever server the customer had. Sometimes powerful, sometimes not. It had to be light.

What We Got Wrong

No centralized logging. Each service logged to its own file. When a problem spanned multiple services, we’d open 4–5 terminal windows, tail different log files, and try to match timestamps by eye. A correlation ID flowing through all services would have saved us hours. We didn’t implement one because we didn’t know it was a pattern.

No service discovery. Hardcoded IPs and ports in config files. Fine for a few deployments, painful for dozens. Every new customer site meant manually editing configuration.

gSOAP for everything. We used it because we knew it, not because it was the best fit. The namespace collisions, the XML overhead, the code generation friction. A lighter protocol would have been better, but the C++ ecosystem in 2013 didn’t offer many alternatives.

No health checks or circuit breakers. If the user service went down, the alerting service would keep trying to call it and eventually time out. No graceful degradation, no automatic recovery detection. We handled it with manual monitoring and restarts.

Why It Worked Anyway

Three people, 15 services, SOAP over gSOAP, CentOS, no containers, no orchestration, manual on-premise deployments. Sounds like it shouldn’t work. But it did, for years. Here’s why:

The boundaries were obvious. Cameras are not users. Users are not alerts. Alerts are not recordings. We didn’t need Domain-Driven Design workshops to figure this out. The previous monolithic project had already shown us where the natural seams were. We just made them explicit.

The team was small enough. Three people sitting next to each other. Communication overhead was zero. We didn’t need API contract management or service catalogs. We talked across the desk.

The number was right. 10–15 services, not 60, not 200. Everyone could hold the full system in their head. Every person could debug every service. There was no “that’s the other team’s service” problem because there was no other team.

On-premise forced simplicity. No cloud auto-scaling, no managed databases, no infinite compute. The product had to run on real hardware at real customer sites. This constraint killed over-engineering before it started. If it couldn’t run on a single server, it was too complex.

What I Realized Later

When Docker and Kubernetes exploded in 2017–2018 and “microservice architecture” became the thing everyone was talking about, I realized we’d been doing it for years. Different tools, same principles: independent deployment, domain-based separation, separate data ownership, process isolation.

The 2018 version came with an ecosystem we didn’t have: containerization, orchestration, distributed tracing, service meshes, circuit breakers. Tools that solve real problems. But tools that also add real complexity. We shipped a working product without any of them.

I’ve since worked on much larger systems with many more services, Kubernetes, Kafka, the full modern stack. The honest comparison: 15 well-bounded services with simple communication was easier to operate than larger architectures with sophisticated tooling. More services doesn’t mean better architecture. It usually means more things that can break.

When Splitting Actually Makes Sense

From doing this more than once:

When you’ve already built the monolith. We built the monolithic version first. It taught us where the real boundaries were. When we built the product, we already knew which modules belonged together and which didn’t. Starting with microservices on day one is guessing. Starting after you’ve seen the domain is informed.

When modules have different lifecycles. Our camera integration changed every week as we added new brands. Authentication changed once a quarter. Forcing them into the same build and deployment cycle was the actual problem.

When the domain boundaries are obvious. If you have to argue about where to draw the line, maybe the line doesn’t exist yet. Our boundaries were clear because cameras, users, alerts, and recordings are genuinely different things with different data and different logic.

When you can keep the number small. 10–15 services for 3 engineers worked. Each person understood every service. The moment you have services that nobody fully understands, you’ve gone too far.

If none of these apply to you, I wrote another post about why you probably don’t need microservices at all. (Link coming when both posts are published.)

Martin Fowler & James Lewis: Microservices (2014)
Martin Fowler: MonolithFirst
gSOAP C++ Namespace Issues (Community Thread)
Sam Newman: Building Microservices (O’Reilly)

content:
I Mined Bitcoin in 2012 on an NVIDIA Tesla GPU. Then a Hard Drive Died.

The most expensive hard drive I never bought was the one I bought instead of Bitcoin.

A GPU that survived, a hard drive that didn’t, and 0.7 Bitcoin somewhere in between.

It was late 2012. I’d just started my first real engineering job. I was 22, excited about everything, and sitting in front of a Dell workstation with an NVIDIA Tesla GPU jammed inside it. The card was the size of a small country. No display output, no fan shroud, just raw compute. We used it for CUDA programming: face recognition, license plate detection, video analytics. Serious work. The kind of work where you compile something and go make tea.

One afternoon, a coworker walked up to my desk.

“Have you heard of Bitcoin?”

I had not.

He explained it to me like I was five, which was appropriate because my understanding of economics was roughly at that level. There’s a program. You run it on your computer. It does math. The math earns you money. The money shows up on a website.

“How much money?”

“Bitcoin is around 11 dollars right now.”

Eleven dollars. A movie ticket. A mediocre lunch. For doing math. On a computer I already had.

The Experiment

We installed whatever mining software was popular at the time (I honestly cannot remember the name). Pointed it at the Tesla card. Hit start. The same GPU that spent its weekdays detecting faces in surveillance footage and reading license plates from blurry traffic cameras was now doing math for strangers on the internet. The workstation started humming in a way that made the facilities guy look over from his desk.

After a day or two, we checked the mining pool website. About 4 or 5 dollars had accumulated. We looked at each other with the grin of two guys who had just discovered free money.

“Let’s leave it running over the weekend,” my coworker said.

Brilliant plan. Forty-eight hours of uninterrupted GPU mining. We’d come back Monday to a small fortune. Or at least enough to buy lunch.

Monday

We walked in Monday morning. The workstation was off.

Not sleeping. Not in standby. Off. Dead. The kind of off where you press the power button and nothing happens, then press it again harder as if force helps with electronics.

My first thought, and I’m not proud of this, was not about the work we might have lost. It was: “Please don’t let the Tesla card be dead.” That GPU was worth more than my monthly salary.

We opened the case. Tried different power configurations. Swapped cables. Nothing. Then we put in a spare hard drive, and the machine booted. The old disk had died. Probably already on its way out, and a weekend of continuous GPU mining at full load was the final push.

The Tesla was fine. The disk was toast. And with it, whatever Bitcoin we’d accumulated over the weekend.

The $180 Fix

It was lunchtime. We walked to the nearest electronics store and bought a hard drive for about $180. Came back, installed the OS, restored everything, got the workstation back to its original state. Work machine first, mining experiment second.

Then I remembered: the mining pool. The website should still have our balance. We logged in.

Seven or eight dollars. That’s what was sitting there.

I did the math that any reasonable person would do in that moment. We had just spent $180 on a hard drive. We had earned $7. The net result of our Bitcoin mining career was negative $173.

“This is stupid,” I said. “We just lost money on free money.”

We closed the browser tab. I never opened that website again. I don’t even remember which mining pool it was.

The Math I Wish I Hadn’t Done

Bitcoin averaged around $11 in October 2012. Seven or eight dollars in the pool meant we were sitting on roughly 0.7 BTC.

We closed the tab on 0.7 Bitcoin.

But that’s not the part that really stings. The part that stings is the $180.

If instead of buying a hard drive to mine Bitcoin, we had just bought Bitcoin with that $180, we’d have gotten around 16 BTC. Bitcoin has touched $140,000 since then. I’ll let you do that multiplication yourself. I did it once, stared at the ceiling for a while, and decided to never do it again.

We had $180. We had heard of Bitcoin. We understood it was digital money. And we chose to spend $180 on a spinning metal disk so we could mine $7 worth of it.

As for that 0.7 BTC still sitting in whatever mining pool we used, I don’t even remember the name. If you ran that pool in 2012 and somehow still have records of an NVIDIA Tesla that mined for four days in October, call me. I’ll buy you a hard drive.

The Guy Who Told Me About Bitcoin

My coworker who introduced me to Bitcoin? He didn’t buy any either. Neither did anyone else in the office. We were all engineers working with NVIDIA Tesla GPUs, literally the best hardware for mining at the time. We had the tools, the knowledge, and the timing. We had everything except the imagination to take it seriously.

Because in 2012, Bitcoin wasn’t an investment. It was a curiosity. Something a guy told you about at lunch. You tried it for a weekend, lost a hard drive, and moved on.

Nobody was wrong for not buying Bitcoin in 2012. Everyone had the same information and almost nobody acted on it. The few who did and held on were either visionary or just forgot their wallet passwords.

What I Actually Took Away

I don’t tell this story as an investment lesson. “You should have bought Bitcoin” is the most useless advice in history because it only works backwards.

But I do think about it when I see something new and dismiss it too quickly. We had the right timing. Bitcoin was $11. We were GPU engineers. The setup was perfect. What we got wrong wasn’t the opportunity, it was the approach. We tried to extract value from it in the most literal, mechanical way possible (run program, get money) instead of stepping back and asking a bigger question: what does it mean that strangers on the internet are willing to pay $11 for something that only exists as math?

If we’d asked that question, maybe we wouldn’t have closed the tab.

Or maybe we still would have. Eleven dollars for magic internet money sounded ridiculous in 2012. To be fair, it still kind of does. It just sounds ridiculous at a much higher price now.

The hard drive, by the way, worked great for years.

I’m Burak Hamuryen, a Senior Software Engineer in Berlin with 14+ years of experience building distributed systems, real-time video processing, and cloud-native platforms. More at hamuryen.com.
